purpose: The ways a running swift program can HOLD layer-1 content. Not layer 1 (the data is fixed), not layer 3 (no operations beyond load-and-read-back), not the type system.
reference: language knowledge, checked against ../type_vocabulary/raw/swift.types.json as a candidate checklist only (superseded node; not a decision instrument).

nothing.note: absence spelled as a case of a two-case shape, so the hole has a declared wrapped kind.
the empty tuple; a value carrying nothing, distinct from an absent value.

truth.note: two values, no numeric side; Swift refuses to treat Bool as an Int.

whole.note: platform word-width signed integer (64-bit here); the default whole-number holder.
signed 32-bit; the narrow end of the fixed-width camp.
unsigned 64-bit; reaches u64 max, refuses anything below zero.
signed 64-bit fixed width, explicit rather than platform-dependent like Int.

fractional.note: IEEE double; the default fractional holder.
IEEE single; holds every base value at lower precision.

text.note: a run of unicode extended grapheme clusters; the default text holder.
text taken apart into grapheme clusters; a clef or an e-acute-plus-combining-mark can still be one element.
holds text only as utf-8 bytes; the grapheme clusters are gone until decoded.
a view into a String's storage rather than an owned buffer; the literal form still needs a String to view.

sequence.note: growable ordered run, one declared element kind.
a window onto an existing array's storage, not a new buffer; length known at run time.

probes.empty:
let base0: [Int] = []
let v: ArraySlice<Int> = base0[...]
probes.base:
let base1: [Int] = [1, 2, 3]
let v: ArraySlice<Int> = base1[...]
probes.strs:
let base2: [String] = ["a", "b"]
let v: ArraySlice<String> = base2[...]
probes.mixed:
let base3: [Int] = [1, "two", 3.0, true, nil]
let v: ArraySlice<Int> = base3[...]
probes.bigint:
let base4: [Int] = [9223372036854775808]
let v: ArraySlice<Int> = base4[...]

sequence.note: the same growable run with bridging to Objective-C ruled out; one declared element kind.

fixed length, and each position may be a different kind; the swift sequence holder that takes the mixed row. A single-element tuple has no literal spelling at all — a trailing comma is a parse error, not a one-tuple.
holds the elements but not their order and not repeats; one declared, hashable element kind.

keyed.note: name to element, no order kept.
keyed.read: ({ () -> String in let ks = v.keys.sorted(); return ks.joined(separator: ",") + "|\(v.count)" })()

keyed.spelling: struct R { var a: Int }; R(a: 1)
keyed.note: names fixed when the shape is declared, not when the data arrives; swift allows the struct declaration right inside the probe, but the odd keys are still not spellable as property names.

probes.flat:
struct R3 { var a: Int; var b: Int; var c: Int }
let v = R3(a: 1, b: 2, c: 3)
probes.intlike:
struct RI { var 1: String; var b: Int }
let v = RI(1: "string-one-key", b: 2)
probes.emptykey:
struct RE { var : String }
let v = RE(: "empty-string key")
probes.nested:
struct RN { var outer: [String: [Int]] }
let v = RN(outer: ["inner": [1, 2]])

keyed.spelling: class C { var a: Int }; C(a: 1)
keyed.note: the reference-type field bag; same identifier refusal as the struct entry, but String(describing:) does surface the fields for a plain class where it only gave the type name for a C# class.

probes.flat:
class C3 { var a: Int; var b: Int; var c: Int; init(a: Int, b: Int, c: Int) { self.a = a; self.b = b; self.c = c } }
let v = C3(a: 1, b: 2, c: 3)
probes.intlike:
class CI { var 1: String; var b: Int; init() { self.1 = "string-one-key"; self.b = 2 } }
let v = CI()
probes.emptykey:
class CE { var : String; init() { self. = "empty-string key" } }
let v = CE()
probes.nested:
class CN { var outer: [String: [Int]]; init(outer: [String: [Int]]) { self.outer = outer } }
let v = CN(outer: ["inner": [1, 2]])

nesting.note: nesting by repeating the same holder; every level must carry the same declared kind.
erases the value kind to Any; the one keyed holder that takes elements of mixed forms and mixed depths.

probes.mixed_depth: let v: [String: Any] = ["a": [1, [2, ["b": [2, nil] as [Any?]]] as [Any]], "c": true]

nesting.spelling: indirect enum Node { case whole(Int), seq([Node]), ... }
nesting.note: a hand-written sum shape; the only swift holder that takes every layer-1 form in one element position, which is what mixed nesting needs. indirect lets a case hold the enum's own kind.

probes.seq_in_seq:
indirect enum Node { case null, truth(Bool), whole(Int), text(String), seq([Node]), map([String: Node]) }
let v = Node.seq([Node.seq([Node.whole(1), Node.whole(2)]), Node.seq([Node.whole(3), Node.whole(4)])])
probes.seq_in_map:
indirect enum Node { case null, truth(Bool), whole(Int), text(String), seq([Node]), map([String: Node]) }
let v = Node.map(["outer": Node.map(["inner": Node.seq([Node.whole(1), Node.whole(2)])])])
probes.mixed_depth:
indirect enum Node { case null, truth(Bool), whole(Int), text(String), seq([Node]), map([String: Node]) }
let v = Node.seq([Node.whole(1), Node.seq([Node.whole(2), Node.map(["k": Node.text("t")])]), Node.truth(true), Node.null])

identity.note: copy-on-write value semantics: two array positions start by sharing storage, but writing through one triggers a copy before the mutation, so the other position never sees it. A struct also has no reference identity, so even a bare equality check can only ever answer distinct. A struct is not allowed to store an instance of itself, so the cycle probe is a refused attempt.

probes.cycle:
struct Loop { var name: String; var selfRef: Loop }
let r = "cycle"

identity.note: reference types default to shared storage; === compares object identity directly, and an optional self-reference field can point back at its own instance.
an Array of a class kind stores references, so two positions can name one object, and a class can even hold an array containing itself.
